analysis.one_liner: Bans insurance companies from denying, limiting, or pricing coverage based on a person's status as a victim of abuse.
analysis.headline: A bill protecting insurance applicants from discrimination over past abuse, backed by 69 House cosponsors from both parties, died in committee without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred health, life, disability, and property insurers from denying, canceling, or limiting coverage, or charging higher premiums, because an applicant or policyholder had been or was perceived to have been the victim of domestic or family abuse. It also would have kept insurers from using or sharing information about a person's abuse history for purposes unrelated to care, required written explanations for adverse decisions, and let victims sue insurers in court, with the Federal Trade Commission empowered to investigate violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of domestic, family, or intimate-partner abuse — overwhelmingly, though not exclusively, women — who in the mid-1990s could be denied health coverage, dropped from a plan, or charged higher premiums when an insurer learned of past abuse, and who could lose coverage entirely when they left an abuser's insurance plan. The bill would have given them the right to keep coverage for 18 months after separating from an abuser's plan, sue for damages, and recover attorney fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of domestic and family abuse

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insurers and health carriers from denying, refusing to renew, canceling, limiting, or adding a premium surcharge to any policy because the applicant or insured is, has been, or may be a victim of abuse [S3].

Bars insurers from terminating health coverage of an abuse victim simply because the policy was in an abuser's name and the couple divorced or separated; the victim must be offered at least 18 months of continued coverage (the abuser or victim may pay the premium) [S3].

Prohibits insurers from using, disclosing, or transferring information about a person's abuse status or abuse-related medical condition for any purpose unrelated to direct health care, unless required by a regulator, a court, or abuse-reporting laws [S3].
Requires insurers to give a written, specific explanation — not a reference to general underwriting guidelines — for any adverse action against a victim of abuse [S3].

Creates a private right of action: a victim can sue in federal or state court for injunctive relief, compensatory or $5,000 statutory damages per violation, punitive damages, and attorney and expert witness fees; the Federal Trade Commission may also investigate insurers and issue cease-and-desist orders [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The insurance industry — health carriers, health plans, and life, disability, and property-casualty insurers — loses underwriting discretion it used to screen out or surcharge applicants with an abuse history, and faces FTC enforcement and lawsuits. Insurers argue that reduced risk selection spreads costs across all policyholders through somewhat higher premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state insurance regulation and imposes a federal mandate on all lines of insurance, with FTC enforcement — an expansion of federal control over an industry traditionally regulated by the states [S3].

The private right of action carries $5,000 statutory damages for each violation plus attorney fees, which insurers would argue invites litigation costs that get passed to other policyholders through premiums [S3].

Requiring continuation of coverage for 18 months after an abuser's plan ends adds a mandated benefit; the bill allows the insurer to require the victim to pay the full premium, which can be a heavy cost for someone leaving an abuser [S3].

The bill carves out life insurance: a life insurer may still decline a policy where the applicant is an abuser designated as beneficiary or lacks an insurable interest, an acknowledgment that blunt prohibitions don't fit every line of insurance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is straightforward and targeted at a documented problem of the era — insurers denying or pricing coverage against abuse victims. The main costs are the federal preemption of state insurance regulation, litigation exposure from statutory damages and fee-shifting, and modest premium pressure from reduced risk selection. The bill's definitions are broad (covering 'may be' a subject of abuse and perceived status), which insurers would say creates compliance uncertainty; the written-reasons and privacy provisions add administrative burden. On balance it is a consumer-protection bill whose costs fall on insurers and are partly spread to other policyholders.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and the Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee, then sent to three subcommittees, where it sat until the 104th Congress ended — no markup, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Bernard Sanders (I-VT) introduced the bill on November 16, 1995, joined by Representatives Morella, Wyden, and DeFazio [S3].
The bill gathered 69 cosponsors — 66 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 Independent [S4].
On the day of introduction it was referred to the Commerce Committee and in addition to the Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee [S5].

Within three weeks it was split among three subcommittees — Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials; Health and Environment; and Employer-Employee Relations — a common way for a bill to be divided among panels with jurisdiction [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no subcommittee or full committee markup, no floor vote. The Congress ended January 3, 1997, and the bill died [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The insurance industry came out ahead: it kept full discretion to deny, limit, or surcharge coverage based on abuse history, and victims of abuse remained exposed to coverage denials and loss of coverage when leaving an abuser's plan.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, who kept their underwriting discretion

industries.industry: Health insurers and health plans (including HMOs and employer group plans)
industries.note: The bill bans the practice at the time of denying or dropping coverage for victims of abuse and forbids treating abuse history as a pre-existing risk, removing a way to exclude costly enrollees. It also makes them the channel through which victims maintain coverage after leaving an abuser's plan.

They lose the ability to deny, limit, or surcharge policies over an applicant's abuse status, and face FTC investigation and lawsuits, but keep a narrow exception to decline life policies where an abuser is the prospective owner-beneficiary.

industries.industry: Insurance agents, brokers, adjusters, and third-party administrators
industries.note: The bill's definition of 'insurer' explicitly includes them, so the prohibitions on discrimination and on disclosing abuse information reach the whole distribution and claims-handling chain.
